\framekicker{Learning outcomes}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Session Objectives}
\leadpar{By the end of this session, participants can:}
\begin{isteps}
\item Frame a business problem as the right \textbf{kind of machine learning task} --- including recognising when machine learning is \textbf{not} the answer.
\item Name the \textbf{two hypotheses} you make silently at the start of every project, and what it means if either is false.
\item Design collection and annotation so the data \textbf{represents production}, and recognise \textbf{sampling bias}, \textbf{target leaks}, and \textbf{concept drift}.
\item Choose a success measure, then choose the \textbf{last-layer activation, loss, and metrics} that match it.
\item Run the three development stages: \textbf{beat a baseline $\rightarrow$ scale up until it overfits $\rightarrow$ regularise and tune}.
\item Choose a deployment route --- \textbf{REST API, on device, or in the browser} --- and optimise the model for inference.
\item Set stakeholder expectations in \textbf{false-positive and false-negative} terms rather than "98\% accurate".
\end{isteps}

\begin{iquote}
\quotetext{Model development is only one step in the machine learning workflow, and if you ask us, it's not the most difficult one. The hardest things in machine learning are framing problems and collecting, annotating, and cleaning data.}\quotecite{Chollet \& Watson, section 6.2}

\coursesection{01}{Defining the task}{You cannot do good work without deeply understanding the context.}

\framekicker{Section 6.1.1}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Four questions to keep at the front of your mind}
\begin{isteps}
\item \textbf{What will the input data be? What are you trying to predict?} You can only learn to predict something you have training data for. \hilite{Data availability is usually the limiting factor here.}
\item \textbf{What type of task is this?} Binary? Multiclass? Scalar regression? Segmentation? Ranking? Or --- quite possibly --- \textbf{machine learning is not the best way} and plain statistics would serve better.
\item \textbf{What do existing solutions look like?} Perhaps a hand-crafted algorithm full of nested \inlinecode{if} statements. Perhaps a person doing it manually today. Understand what is already in place.
\item \textbf{Are there particular constraints?} End-to-end encryption may force the model onto the user's phone. Latency may force it onto an embedded device at the factory rather than a remote server.
\end{isteps}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 6.1.1}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Why the third question matters more than it looks}
\begin{iband}[amber]
In most real projects the baseline is \textbf{not} "random". It is a rules-based system that has been running for years and that people already trust --- and \hilite{that is a much harder thing to beat}
\end{iband}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}It is also the thing you will be compared against when the project is reviewed, so it should be measured properly at the start rather than described from memory.\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 6.1.1}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{The seven examples, mapped to task types}
\begin{itable}{>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.2068\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.2632\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.47\textwidth}}
\thead{Project} & \thead{Task type} & \thead{Note} \\ \midrule
Photo search & \textbf{Multiclass, multilabel} & --- \\
Spam & \textbf{Binary} & Becomes \textbf{three-way} if \textit{offensive content} is a separate class. \\
Music recommendation & \hilite{Not deep learning} & Better handled by \textbf{matrix factorisation} (collaborative filtering). \\
Credit-card fraud & \textbf{Binary} & --- \\
Click-through rate & \textbf{Scalar regression} & --- \\
Defective biscuits & \textbf{Binary} & But needs \textbf{object detection} first, to crop the biscuits out of the raw images. The book notes that \textit{anomaly detection} \hilite{would not fit here} \\
Archaeological sites & \textbf{Image similarity ranking} & Retrieve images most like known sites. \\
\end{itable}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 6.1.1}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Two lessons hiding in that table}
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.494\textwidth}
\begin{icardwarn}
\cardh{Some problems are not deep learning problems}
The music recommender is better served by collaborative filtering. Recognising that early saves months.
\end{icardwarn}
\end{minipage}%
\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.494\textwidth}
\begin{icardwarn}
\cardh{Some need two models in sequence}
The biscuit case needs detection before classification. Framing it as one model would fail quietly.
\end{icardwarn}
\end{minipage}%
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Both are missed routinely when a team jumps straight to modelling.\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 6.1.1}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{The two hypotheses you are making silently}
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.494\textwidth}
\begin{icardaccent}
\cardh{Your targets can be predicted from your inputs}
That the relationship exists at all.
\end{icardaccent}
\end{minipage}%
\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.494\textwidth}
\begin{icardaccent}
\cardh{Your data is sufficiently informative}
That it is enough to learn that relationship.
\end{icardaccent}
\end{minipage}%
\begin{iband}[rose]
Until you have a working model these are \textbf{merely hypotheses}. Assembling examples of X and targets Y \hilite{does not mean X contains enough information to predict Y}
\end{iband}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}The book's example: predicting a stock's movement from its recent price history is \textbf{unlikely to succeed}, because price history does not contain much predictive information.\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}
\note{Test both hypotheses in the framing meeting, not after three months of modelling. This is the single biggest time-saver in the chapter.}

\framekicker{Section 6.1.1 $\cdot$ ethics}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Technology is never neutral}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}The book places its ethics note \textbf{in the framing stage}, not at the end. Its example: \textit{"building an AI that rates the trustworthiness of someone from a picture of their face"}.\par}\vskip 4pt
\begin{isteps}
\item \textbf{The validity is already in doubt} --- it is not clear why trustworthiness would be reflected in a face.
\item Collecting a dataset would amount to \textbf{recording the biases and prejudices of the people labelling the pictures}.
\item A model trained on it would merely \textbf{encode those same biases into a black-box algorithm} --- which gives them a thin veneer of legitimacy.
\end{isteps}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 6.1.1 $\cdot$ ethics}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Why the veneer is the dangerous part}
\begin{iquote}
\quotetext{In a largely tech-illiterate society like ours, "The AI algorithm said this person cannot be trusted" strangely appears to carry more weight and objectivity than "John Smith said this person cannot be trusted" --- despite the former being a learned approximation of the latter.}\quotecite{Chollet \& Watson, section 6.1.1}
\end{iquote}
\begin{iband}[rose]
\textbf{Technical choices are also ethical choices.} If your work has any impact on the world, that impact has a moral direction --- so \hilite{be deliberate about the values your work supports}
\end{iband}
\end{frame}
\note{Easy to make concrete for any audience: eligibility scoring, pricing, and customer flagging can all launder historical bias and give it an objective face.}

\framekicker{Section 6.1.2}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Collecting data is the expensive part --- and the highest-return one}
\begin{iquote}
\quotetext{If you get an extra 50 hours to spend on a project, chances are that the most effective way to allocate them is to collect more data, rather than search for incremental modeling improvements.}\quotecite{Chollet \& Watson, section 6.1.2}
\end{iquote}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}The point that data matters more than algorithms was made most famously in a 2009 Google paper, \textit{"The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Data"} --- itself a play on Eugene Wigner's 1960 title. That predates the popularity of deep learning, and the rise of deep learning has \hilite{only increased the importance of data}\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 6.1.2}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Who should do the annotating}
\begin{itable}{>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.2444\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.3384\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.3572\textwidth}}
\thead{Option} & \thead{Upside} & \thead{Risk} \\ \midrule
\textbf{Annotate it yourself} & Full control over quality. & Slow and costly in time. \\
\textbf{Crowdsourcing} (e.g. Mechanical Turk) & Inexpensive and scales well. & Annotations may end up \hilite{quite noisy} \\
\textbf{A specialist labelling company} & Saves time and money. & Takes away control. \\
\end{itable}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Your annotation process determines the quality of your targets, which in turn determines the quality of your model. It deserves the same scrutiny as the architecture.\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 6.1.2}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Three questions that decide which option}
\begin{ibullets}
\item \textbf{Do the labellers need to be subject-matter experts?} Cat versus dog can be done by anyone; dog breeds need specialised knowledge; annotating CT scans of fractures \hilite{pretty much requires a medical degree}.
\item \textbf{If expertise is needed, can you train people?} If not, how will you get access to the relevant experts at all?
\item \textbf{Do you yourself understand how the experts arrive at the annotations?} If not, your dataset becomes a black box and manual feature engineering is closed to you --- not fatal, but limiting.
\end{ibullets}
\begin{iband}[signal]
And decide early what software will record the annotations. Productive annotation tooling \textbf{saves a great deal of time}, so it is worth investing in \hilite{at the start of a project, not the middle}
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 6.1.2}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Non-representative data --- the cardinal sin}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}The book's example: an app that identifies a dish from a photo, trained on pictures from an image-sharing network popular with food enthusiasts. Test accuracy well over 90\%.\par}\vskip 4pt
\begin{iband}[rose]
After release: \textbf{wrong 8 times out of 10}. User photos --- random dishes, random restaurants, random phones --- \hilite{look nothing like} the professional, well-lit, appetising pictures it was trained on.
\end{iband}
\begin{ibullets}
\item Where possible, collect data \textbf{directly from the environment the model will be used in}.
\item A review sentiment model belongs on new IMDB reviews --- not Yelp reviews, not tweets.
\item If training on production data is impossible, \textbf{understand exactly how they differ} and correct for it actively.
\end{ibullets}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 6.1.2}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Sampling bias: DEWEY DEFEATS TRUMAN}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}\textbf{Sampling bias} is the subtlest form: your collection process interacts with the thing you are trying to predict.\par}\vskip 4pt
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}On election night in 1948 the \textit{Chicago Tribune} printed the headline \textbf{"DEWEY DEFEATS TRUMAN"}. By morning Truman had won. The editor had trusted a telephone survey --- but telephone users in 1948 \hilite{were not a representative sample of voters}. They were likelier to be richer, more conservative, and to vote for Dewey.\par}\vskip 4pt
\begin{iband}[amber]
Every phone survey now accounts for this. That does not make sampling bias a thing of the past --- \hilite{only a thing pollsters are now aware of}
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 6.1.2}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Concept drift, and how long a model lives}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.92\linewidth,height=0.60\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figs/ch06-drift.tex.pdf}
\end{center}
\vskip 3pt{\color{ink3}\fontsize{7.4}{9.4}\selectfont The book's own figures. The most adversarial problem is the one that goes stale fastest.\par}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}\textbf{Concept drift} is when the properties of production data change over time, gradually degrading the model. The IMDB dataset was collected in 2011; a model trained on it does worse on 2020 reviews than on 2012 ones, because vocabulary, expressions, and genres move.\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 6.1.2}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{The assumption underneath every deployed model}
\begin{iband}[rose]
Machine learning can only memorise patterns \textbf{present in the training data}. Using a model trained on the past to predict the future assumes \textbf{the future will behave like the past}. \hilite{Often it does not.}
\end{iband}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Handling fast drift requires continuous data collection, annotation, and retraining --- which is a staffing decision as much as a technical one.\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 6.1.3}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Understand your data before you model it}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Treating a dataset as a black box is \textbf{bad practice}. Before training anything, explore and visualise.\par}\vskip 4pt
\begin{isteps}
\item Images or text? \textbf{Look at a few samples directly}, with their labels.
\item Numeric features? \textbf{Plot the histograms} to feel the ranges and frequencies.
\item Location data? \textbf{Put it on a map.} Do patterns appear?
\item Any \textbf{missing values}? They must be handled during preparation.
\item A classification task? \textbf{Print the count per class.} If it is not balanced, that has to be accounted for.
\item Check for \textbf{target leaks}.
\end{isteps}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 6.1.3}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Target leaking, and the one question that catches it}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.92\linewidth,height=0.60\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figs/ch06-leakcheck.tex.pdf}
\end{center}
\vskip 3pt{\color{ink3}\fontsize{7.4}{9.4}\selectfont Ask it of every column, not just the suspicious ones.\par}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}The book's example: training on medical records to predict whether someone will be treated for cancer, where the records include the feature \textit{"this person has been diagnosed with cancer"}.\par}\vskip 4pt
\begin{iband}[amber]
The common real-world shape: \textbf{fields filled in later by an operator} --- handling status, closure code, follow-up notes. None of them exist \hilite{at the moment the model has to decide}
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 6.1.4}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Choosing a measure of success}
\begin{iquote}
\quotetext{To control something, you need to be able to observe it. To achieve success on a project, you must first define what you mean by success.}\quotecite{Chollet \& Watson, section 6.1.4}
\end{iquote}
\begin{itable}{>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.376\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.564\textwidth}}
\thead{Problem shape} & \thead{Common metrics} \\ \midrule
\textbf{Balanced} classification & Accuracy, and \textbf{AUC} of the ROC curve. \\
\textbf{Imbalanced}, ranking, multilabel & \textbf{Precision and recall}, or a metric counting false/true positives and negatives. \\
Neither of the above & It is not unusual to have to \textbf{define your own metric}. \\
\end{itable}
\begin{iband}[signal]
The metric guides \textbf{every technical decision} in the project, so it must align directly with the higher-level goal --- \hilite{the customer's business success}
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\coursesection{02}{Developing a model}{The part every tutorial covers --- and not the hardest one.}

\framekicker{Section 6.2.1}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Vectorisation and normalisation}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Neural networks do not ingest raw data. Whatever you have --- sound, images, text --- must become float tensors first, and those tensors must have sane ranges.\par}\vskip 4pt
\icode{python}{the two properties you want}{listings/ch06-01.py}
\begin{iband}[signal]
Feeding in large values (multi-digit integers) or heterogeneous ones (one feature 0--1, another 100--200) triggers \textbf{large gradient updates that prevent the network from converging}.
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 6.2.1}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Missing values: categorical and numerical differ}
\begin{itable}{>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.2444\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.6956\textwidth}}
\thead{Missing value in a\ldots{}} & \thead{What to do} \\ \midrule
\textbf{Categorical} feature & Safe to create a \textbf{new category meaning "missing"}. The model will learn what that implies about the target on its own. \\
\textbf{Numerical} feature & \textbf{Avoid an arbitrary value such as 0} --- it can create a discontinuity in the latent space. Use the \textbf{mean or median}, or train a model to predict the value from the other features. \\
\end{itable}
\begin{iband}[amber]
A subtle trap: if you \textbf{expect} missing categorical values at test time but trained on complete data, the network \hilite{never learned to ignore them}. Fix it by generating training samples with holes --- duplicate some rows and drop the fields you expect to lose.
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 6.2.3 -- 6.2.5}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Model development is three stages, in order}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.92\linewidth,height=0.60\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figs/ch06-stages.tex.pdf}
\end{center}
\vskip 3pt{\color{ink3}\fontsize{7.4}{9.4}\selectfont Doing them out of order --- regularising before you can overfit --- wastes the most time.\par}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 6.2.3}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Stage 1 --- beat a baseline}
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.3253\textwidth}
\begin{icardaccent}
\cardh{Feature engineering}
Filter out uninformative features, and use knowledge of the problem to build likely-useful new ones.
\end{icardaccent}
\end{minipage}%
\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.3253\textwidth}
\begin{icardaccent}
\cardh{The right architecture priors}
Densely connected? ConvNet? Recurrent? Transformer? Or is deep learning even the right approach here?
\end{icardaccent}
\end{minipage}%
\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.3253\textwidth}
\begin{icardaccent}
\cardh{A good enough training configuration}
Which loss function? What batch size and learning rate?
\end{icardaccent}
\end{minipage}%
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}The goal at this stage is \textbf{statistical power}: a small model that beats a simple baseline. Nothing more.\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 6.2.3 $\cdot$ table 6.1}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{The reference table for that third choice}
\begin{itable}{>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.2444\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.1692\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.2444\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.282\textwidth}}
\thead{Task} & \thead{Last-layer activation} & \thead{Loss function} & \thead{Metrics} \\ \midrule
Binary classification & Sigmoid & Binary crossentropy & Binary accuracy, ROC AUC \\
Multiclass, single-label & Softmax & Categorical crossentropy & Categorical accuracy, top-k, ROC AUC \\
Multiclass, multi-label & Sigmoid & Binary crossentropy & Binary accuracy, ROC AUC \\
Regression & None & Mean squared error & Mean absolute error \\
\end{itable}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 6.2.3}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Why you optimise a proxy instead of the metric you care about}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}A loss function must be computable from a single mini-batch --- ideally from a single data point --- and it must be \textbf{differentiable}, or backpropagation cannot run.\par}\vskip 4pt
\begin{iband}[signal]
\textbf{ROC AUC satisfies neither}, so it cannot be optimised directly. In classification we optimise a proxy --- usually crossentropy --- \hilite{hoping that as crossentropy falls, ROC AUC rises}
\end{iband}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}For most problems there are existing templates. You are not the first person to build a spam detector or an image classifier, so \textbf{research the prior art} before inventing.\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 6.2.4}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Stage 2 --- scale up until it overfits}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Statistical power is not enough. Is the model \textit{powerful enough}? A logistic regression has statistical power on MNIST but cannot solve it well.\par}\vskip 4pt
\begin{ibullets}
\item Add layers.
\item Make the layers bigger.
\item Train for more epochs.
\end{ibullets}
\begin{iband}[signal]
The ideal model sits \textbf{exactly on the border} between underfitting and overfitting. \hilite{To find where the border is, you must cross it.}
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 6.2.5}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Stage 3 --- regularise and tune}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}This phase takes the most time: modify, train, evaluate on \textbf{validation} data, modify again, and repeat until the model is as good as it will get.\par}\vskip 4pt
\begin{ibullets}
\item Try different architectures; add or remove layers.
\item Add \textbf{dropout}.
\item If the model is small, add \textbf{L1 or L2 regularisation}.
\item Try different hyperparameters --- units per layer, learning rate.
\item Optionally iterate on \textbf{data curation or feature engineering} again.
\end{ibullets}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Much of this can be automated with hyperparameter tuning software such as \textbf{KerasTuner} (chapter 18).\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 6.2.5}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{The leak that comes back at the end}
\begin{iband}[rose]
Every time you use validation feedback to tune, information leaks into the model. A few times is harmless. Done \textbf{systematically over many iterations}, the model overfits \hilite{to the validation process itself} --- even though no model was ever trained on validation data.
\end{iband}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}So if test performance turns out \textbf{significantly worse} than validation performance, either your validation procedure was not reliable, or you overfitted to it. The remedy is a more reliable protocol --- \textbf{iterated K-fold}.\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}

\coursesection{03}{Deploying your model}{A project does not end at a notebook that saves a trained model.}

\framekicker{Section 6.3.1}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Do not say "98\% accurate"}
\begin{ibullets}
\item Non-specialists often expect the system to \textbf{understand} its task and to exercise human-like common sense.
\item The remedy: \textbf{show examples of how it fails} --- especially misclassifications that look surprising.
\item Avoid abstract statements like \textit{"the model is 98\% accurate"}, which \hilite{most people mentally round up to 100\%}.
\end{ibullets}
\begin{iband}[signal]
Speak in \textbf{false-negative and false-positive rates}, then translate them into daily volumes that a person can picture.
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 6.3.1}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{What that sounds like in practice}
\begin{iquote}
\quotetext{With these settings, the fraud detection model would have a 5\% false-negative rate and a 2.5\% false-positive rate. Every day, an average of 200 valid transactions would be flagged as fraudulent and sent for manual review, and an average of 14 fraudulent transactions would be missed. An average of 266 fraudulent transactions would be correctly caught.}\quotecite{The book's own worked example, section 6.3.1}
\end{iquote}
\begin{iband}[amber]
Also discuss the \textbf{threshold} with stakeholders. Different thresholds give different error rates, and that trade-off \hilite{can only be resolved with deep knowledge of the business context}
\end{iband}
\end{frame}
\note{The most directly usable slide in the chapter. Exercise: have each participant rewrite one accuracy claim from their own project in this form.}

\framekicker{Section 6.3.2}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Three deployment routes}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.92\linewidth,height=0.60\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figs/ch06-deploy.tex.pdf}
\end{center}
\vskip 3pt{\color{ink3}\fontsize{7.4}{9.4}\selectfont The constraints choose the route, not the other way round.\par}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 6.3}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Reading the tree: what each question is really asking}
\begin{itable}{>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.2444\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.4324\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.2632\textwidth}}
\thead{Question} & \thead{Why it comes first} & \thead{Where a yes sends you} \\ \midrule
\textbf{Sensitive data, or poor connectivity?} & This one outranks the others because it is not a performance question. If the data may not leave the device, or there is no reliable link, no amount of latency budget changes the answer. & \textbf{On device} --- TF Lite, ONNX runtime \\
\textbf{Strict latency requirement?} & A REST round trip costs roughly 500 ms before your model does anything. That is fine for a form submission and useless for anything reacting to a camera. & on to the next question \\
\textbf{Move compute to the user?} & Running in the browser costs you nothing per request and costs the user their battery. It also means shipping the model weights, which anyone can then keep. & \textbf{In the browser} --- TensorFlow.js, ONNX JS \\
\end{itable}
\begin{iband}[signal]
\textbf{Every path that answers \textit{no} ends at the REST API}, and that is the right default: one copy of the model, one place to update it, one place to watch. Leave it only when a constraint above forces you to.
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 6.3.2}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{When each route is the right one}
\begin{itable}{>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.1692\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.47\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.3008\textwidth}}
\thead{Route} & \thead{Use it when} & \thead{Example from the book} \\ \midrule
\textbf{REST API} & Reliable internet $\cdot$ no strict latency (round trip $\approx$ \textbf{500 ms}) $\cdot$ input data is not highly sensitive, since it must be decrypted on the server. & Image search, recommender, fraud detection, satellite imagery. \\
\textbf{On device} & Strict latency or poor connectivity $\cdot$ the model can be made small enough $\cdot$ top accuracy is not mission-critical $\cdot$ input data must not be decryptable off-device. & Spam filter inside an end-to-end encrypted chat app; biscuit detection at the factory. \\
\textbf{In the browser} & You want to move compute to the user (server costs drop sharply) $\cdot$ data must stay on their machine $\cdot$ latency matters $\cdot$ it must work offline after download. & The web and desktop versions of the chat app. \\
\end{itable}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 6.3.2}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{One warning about the browser route}
\begin{iband}[rose]
The \textbf{entire model is downloaded to the user's device}. Make sure nothing about it needs to stay confidential --- because given a trained model it is usually possible to \hilite{recover some information about its training data}
\end{iband}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Which means: do not publish a model that was trained on sensitive data, however convenient the deployment would be.\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 6.3.2}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Exporting: TensorFlow Serving and ONNX}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Both work by lifting the weights and the computation graph \textbf{out of the Python program}, so the model can be served from a C++ server, a phone, or a browser.\par}\vskip 4pt
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.485\textwidth}
\icode{python}{TensorFlow SavedModel}{listings/ch06-02.py}

\end{minipage}%
\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.485\textwidth}
\icode{python}{ONNX}{listings/ch06-03.py}

\end{minipage}%
\begin{iband}[signal]
If that sounds like the compilation mechanism from chapter 3, it is: TensorFlow Serving is essentially \hilite{a library for serving \inlinecode{tf.function} graphs with a saved set of weights}
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 6.3.2}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Where those exports run}
\begin{ibullets}
\item \textbf{TensorFlow Lite} --- on-device inference for Android and iOS, ARM CPUs, Raspberry Pi, and some microcontrollers. Same save format as TF Serving. The ONNX runtime also runs on mobile.
\item \textbf{TensorFlow.js} --- runs in the browser and implements almost the whole Keras API (its working name was \textit{WebKeras}). ONNX has its own JavaScript runtime.
\item \textbf{Managed cloud services} such as Cloud AI Platform handle batching, load balancing, and scaling for you.
\end{ibullets}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 6.3.2}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Optimising for inference}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.92\linewidth,height=0.60\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figs/ch06-optimise.tex.pdf}
\end{center}
\vskip 3pt{\color{ink3}\fontsize{7.4}{9.4}\selectfont Both techniques trade a little accuracy for a lot of size and speed.\par}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}\textbf{Pruning} drops the coefficients that contribute least; how much you prune is your lever on the size-versus-accuracy trade-off. \textbf{Quantization} converts float32 weights to int8, giving a model \textbf{four times smaller} that stays near the original accuracy.\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 6.3.2}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Quantization is one line}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Keras exposes it directly on the model, so it can be applied just before export.\par}\vskip 4pt
\icode{python}{the built-in quantize API}{listings/ch06-04.py}
\begin{iband}[signal]
Do this \textbf{before} importing into TensorFlow.js or exporting to TensorFlow Lite --- it matters most where power and memory are tight, \hilite{phones and embedded devices}
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 6.3.3}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Monitoring: pressing the button is not the end}
\begin{isteps}
\item \textbf{Randomised A/B testing.} Send a subset of cases through the new model and keep a control subset on the old process. Once enough cases have run, the difference \hilite{can be attributed to the model} rather than to everything else that changed.
\item \textbf{Regular manual audits} of predictions on production data. Reuse the annotation infrastructure: send a fraction out for labelling and compare.
\item \textbf{When manual audit is impossible}, use alternatives such as user surveys --- the book's suggestion for the spam and abuse flagging system.
\end{isteps}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 6.3.4}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Maintenance starts on launch day}
\begin{iband}[amber]
\textbf{As soon as your model has launched, you should be getting ready to train the next generation that will replace it.}
\end{iband}
\begin{ibullets}
\item Watch for \textbf{changes in production data}. Are new features available? Should the label set be expanded or edited?
\item Keep collecting and annotating, and \textbf{keep improving the annotation pipeline} over time.
\item Pay special attention to samples the current model finds \textbf{difficult} --- those are \hilite{the ones most likely to improve performance}
\end{ibullets}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Summary}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{What has to survive this chapter}
\begin{isteps}
\item \textbf{Define the task first.} Understand the context, the goal, and the constraints; collect and annotate data; choose how success is measured.
\item You always make \textbf{two hypotheses}. Until a model works, neither is proven.
\item \textbf{Technical choices are ethical choices.} Technology is never neutral.
\item \textbf{Data must represent production.} Watch for sampling bias, target leaks, and concept drift.
\item \textbf{Beat a baseline $\rightarrow$ scale up until it overfits $\rightarrow$ regularise and tune.} In that order.
\item \textbf{Deploy according to the constraints} --- API, device, or browser --- then prune and quantize for inference.
\item \textbf{Talk in false positives and false negatives}, not percentages of accuracy.
\item \textbf{No model lasts forever.} Monitor, audit, and prepare the successor from launch day.
\end{isteps}
